title: Winter in Moscow
description: Muggeridge's satire of the Soviet Union and of its Western admirers, drawn from his time in Moscow as the Manchester Guardian's stand-in correspondent in 1932-33: it describes conditions in the 'socialist utopia' and satirises Western journalists' uncritical view of the Soviet regime.
plot_or_argument: Drawing on what Muggeridge saw in Moscow and on his journey to the famine regions, the book describes conditions in the Soviet 'socialist utopia' and satirises the Western journalists whose reports of the regime were uncritical.
narrative_structure: A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the satirical sentence of the journalist with the moralist's edge.
historical_context: Muggeridge went to Moscow in 1932, initially attracted by communism, to stand in for the Manchester Guardian's correspondent William Henry Chamberlin. Travelling to Ukraine and the Caucasus without the permission of the Soviet authorities, he reported the famine in despatches sent in the diplomatic bag; those that were printed, on 25, 27 and 28 March 1933, appeared without his name, while Walter Duranty of the New York Times denied that any famine existed. After this conflict with British newspapers' policy of not provoking the Soviet authorities, Muggeridge returned to novel writing.
literary_significance: The book turned to satire the experience behind Muggeridge's famine reports, which with those of Gareth Jones helped to confirm the extent of the famine; he later called Duranty 'the greatest liar I have met in journalism'. It marks the point at which his politics began to move from an independent socialism towards the conservative religious position of his later career.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1934, as satirical novel, by Malcolm Muggeridge. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Jane Clegg
description: The play of the deserted wife and the suffrage generation. It is a dramatic work of 1913 by St John Ervine; it belongs to Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre and it is catalogued here under Suffrage Play and the Woman's Drama; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
plot_or_argument: Jane Clegg, a wife deserted by her husband, tries to support herself and her children in Belfast while he drifts through England; the play that made Ervine the Ulster dramatist of the new drama and put the woman's question on the stage.
narrative_structure: Three acts, in a Belfast household and its aftermath. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
principal_characters: Jane Clegg; her husband; her children; the neighbours
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the plain Ulster dialogue of the farmhouse and the chapel.
historical_context: Belfast and England in the early 1910s, the suffrage generation and the new drama.
